articles.title: A Failed Policy: Nametags at Govs
paras: For the past two weeks, students across Govs were asked to wear name tags around campus. However, not all students followed the request. The tags were meant to make it easier for students, faculty, and other members of the Govs community to identify one another, especially as new faculty joined the school. While the request had a clear purpose, students' reactions raised questions about how effective the initiative was.
articles.text: For the past two weeks, students across Govs were asked to wear name tags around campus. However, not all students followed the request. The tags were meant to make it easier for students, faculty, and other members of the Govs community to identify one another, especially as new faculty joined the school. While the request had a clear purpose, students' reactions raised questions about how effective the initiative was. The Dean’s team introduced the name tags to help members of the community learn each other’s names and encourage more interaction. The decision was partly influenced by the number of new faculty members joining campus. Ms. Gargano explained there was a “good mix of both” goals: helping people learn names and encouraging members of the community to know one another. For a school where students and faculty interact throughout the day, knowing someone’s name can make approaching them easier. Instead of having to ask someone's name, students could simply look at their tag. However, some students were reluctant to follow the request. Sienna Mercaldi ‘27 said she did not think students took the name tags as seriously as teachers expected. “I haven’t worn a name tag since elementary school,” Sienna said, explaining that she viewed the requirement as something that did not fit naturally into a high school environment. Another concern was the physical size of the name tags. Mr. Nelson pointed out that the name tags were very small, making the names difficult to see from far away. If one of the main purposes of the initiative was to make it easier for people to identify one another, the size of the tags could limit how useful they actually were. Rather than abandoning the goal of creating a welcoming community, Govs could consider other ways to encourage everyone to get to know one another. Activities that bring together different grades and faculty could create opportunities for people to introduce themselves, such as having more Unity Days or combining advisories with other groups. Another option could be a peer leadership program, where groups of 10-15 underclassmen are assigned an older student who can help them adjust to campus and answer questions. Ms. Gargano suggested that the school could try “a different way that is more appealing” in the future. Finding a more natural approach could also still accomplish the school's goal while making students more willing to participate.

Students jumped, danced, and ran frantically in circles to old-timey folk songs, even tapping into their childhood roots with the classic Cotton-Eye Joe routine. On Saturday night, Porter Field was blown up with several inflatables courtesy of Ms. Gargano. These inflatable games included an obstacle course, fighting area, Velcro jumpsuits and a Velcro wall (imagine what happened there), and more! It was an opportunity to watch students smash into inflatable objects and absolutely eat dirt, and it was hilarious. Both square dancing and inflatables were major successes, and students are already looking forward to their return next year! Our first official day back included familiar and new faces, all dressed up. Some say we should wear formal dress more often, while others say we shouldn’t wear it at all. What do you think? The week began with our first real day of classes and ended with the Dummer Cup. Ingham has the lead in points so far. You can hear more about the Dummer Cup in Owen’s article on the next page, where he speaks with students and faculty about how great last Friday night was. Tuesday was particularly fun for the seniors; they departed from campus for Senior Sunrise. Arriving at 5:50 a.m., they made it to the beach just in time. StuCo made great photo frames, the deans provided donuts, and there was plenty of good company. They enjoyed taking photos, hanging out with friends, and watching the sun turn orange. One could say it couldn’t have been better, but every bus wanted to stop at Dunkin on the way back! This action-packed opening week of school set a high-energy tone, promising a great school year ahead. Welcome back, Govs!!

articles.title: Govs vs. Brooks RIVALRY
paras: Almost all Govs students are familiar with our rivalry with Brooks. However, where does that rivalry come from? The Govs-Brooks rivalry is a century old, and the school should make an effort to keep the rivalry vibrant in the years to come.

According to a past Governor article from 2010, it states that the first time the two schools played each other was in a hockey game on December 18, 1931. This was only five years after Brooks had been founded in 1926. So how could a school that was founded in 1926 compete so fiercely with our 1763 founding? And who did we compete with before then?

The Govs-Brooks rivalry is a century old, and the school should make an effort to keep the rivalry vibrant in the years to come. According to a past Governor article from 2010, it states that the first time the two schools played each other was in a hockey game on December 18, 1931. This was only five years after Brooks had been founded in 1926. So how could a school that was founded in 1926 compete so fiercely with our 1763 founding? And who did we compete with before then? Mrs. Slater, the school historian, shared that originally our rival was Belmont Hill. However, when Govs became co-ed in 1971, it became clear that it would no longer make sense to have our rival be an all-boys school. Peter Bragdon, former head of school and Brooks faculty kid, decided that Brooks would be the new major rival. The 2010 Governor article also said that Govs and Brooks didn't originally play each other in football as they feared the schools would only play pranks on one another. However, after the ISL formed in 1948, Brooks became a regular on the teams’ schedules. The relationship between Govs and Brooks involves school spirit, traditions, and a sense of fun that only students can bring. Some of those early traditions were certainly more extreme than what we see today. Govs students used to burn mannequins dressed in Brooks apparel to signify Govs students’ superiority over Brooks students — both academically and athletically. Another tradition involves an athletic competition between the two schools where the losing team would fly the flag of the opposing school that had won. Additionally, students have involved Brooks in many senior pranks, like putting Govs merch all over their school. The reason the Govs-Brooks rivalry has lasted so long is simple: proximity. Unlike a school like St. Georges, Brooks is close enough to feel like a constant competitor. The two schools are only 11.3 miles apart, and outside of sports, they compete for similar incoming students. They are both boarding schools in northern Massachusetts that prioritize athletics, small class sizes, and a close-knit community. As of now, the rivalry between Govs and Brooks feels as though it is a low point. We have lost a lot of previous traditions and playing them in sports almost feels like playing any other school. “Rivalries really encourage school spirit,” said Mrs. Slater. There are bigger crowds at sports games and events. Rivalries are beneficial to sports culture, but they also help to bring a community together. It makes students proud of their school and what they can accomplish.

articles.title: New Doors on Campus
paras: With this year’s new door-locking system, I have witnessed teachers and students stuck behind doors and unable to get through at times of day when punctuality is key. With all the new rules and regulations around campus, adding more factors for being late to class isn’t ideal for students trying to succeed. But the door system is a necessary new reality. Maybe the problem doesn’t lie in the new system but in people who are scared of change.
articles.text: With this year’s new door-locking system, I have witnessed teachers and students stuck behind doors and unable to get through at times of day when punctuality is key. With all the new rules and regulations around campus, adding more factors for being late to class isn’t ideal for students trying to succeed. But the door system is a necessary new reality. Maybe the problem doesn’t lie in the new system but in people who are scared of change. As summer closed, students and faculty returned to campus and a whole new way of navigating the door entries for the buildings. Our Student IDs no longer allow us into buildings; it is a new app on our phones that lets us tap to open doors. Although a new app and new technology sounds fantastic for a school that's been around since the 1700s, it has its upsides and downsides. The new app allows the school to have more control over access to the buildings in order to keep the campus secure. Mr. McGonagill explains, “Change can be scary, but from a security standpoint, the improved technology will definitely benefit the community in the long run.” On the other side, Drew Giguere, ‘27, believes that the new app “takes away a sense of privacy because it tracks you wherever you are going.” From a student perspective, the app could make us feel like we are being monitored too closely and eliminate any sense of freedom we had before. But it allows the school to know where we are at all times and to lock down the buildings when there is a threat to campus. For new students, this added to the challenge of learning their way around a new campus. Cole Cournoyer ‘28 said, “It’s definitely hard to get into buildings, especially transitioning from my old school. Sometimes my phone is dead, or I’m by myself and the system is having trouble while I’m trying to get into the dorm or buildings. It can be frustrating having to wait or figuring it out.” Govs is trying to encourage us to be less dependent on our phones, but needing them on standby at all times contradicts this idea. There are certainly both positive and negative views of the new door lock system. The app’s functionality definitely needs work, as it has glitches. The Govs community just needs to adjust to the change because the app’s intentions are good. The minor glitches that make the student body uncomfortable will be fixed in the future, and we will all benefit from a safer environment.

articles.title: New Policy on Absences
paras: A missed class can happen for many reasons, whether a student oversleeps, has a family emergency, struggles with a mental health issue, or simply forgets an assignment or deadline and does not want to deal with it. With the first month of school already behind them, students are adjusting to the new attendance rules designed to make skipping class harder to get away with. The policy has sparked questions about how the school should balance student accountability with the understanding that some significant reason could be behind a missed class.
articles.text: A missed class can happen for many reasons, whether a student oversleeps, has a family emergency, struggles with a mental health issue, or simply forgets an assignment or deadline and does not want to deal with it. With the first month of school already behind them, students are adjusting to the new attendance rules designed to make skipping class harder to get away with. The policy has sparked questions about how the school should balance student accountability with the understanding that some significant reason could be behind a missed class. Under the new policy created by the dean's team, consequences increase with each unexcused absence. One unexcused absence leads to a Friday night study hall. A second unexcused absence results in a longer Friday night study hall, and three unexcused absences result in "clipboarding.” According to Ms. Gargano, "clipboarding" means checking in on campus on Sunday from 9am to 7pm, signing a sheet every hour to show they are present. Both day students and boarders are expected to follow the same Sunday schedule. The change in rules is meant to make missed classes and the consequences harder to ignore. Mrs. Kingsbury explained the reasoning behind the change: "Every hour a student misses, they owe us back an hour.” Her comment shows that class time is valuable and that students should take responsibility for what they miss. Teachers are frustrated with the lack of consequences for multiple absences. Last year, students seemed to take advantage of the fact that three unexcused absences equaled a Friday night study hall. Students would use two of those three unexcused absences to skip a class if they wanted, avoiding accountability. Mrs. Kingsbury said the new rules bring a different kind of responsibility for staff, but not necessarily more work. Instead, she described it as “different levels of commitment to enforce things.” Some students feel that the policy does not leave enough room before they immediately get in trouble. Ayla Cifric ‘27 and Grace Fyrberg ‘27 said, “We don't particularly think that is fair.” They would prefer a two-strike system. A first absence would serve as their one and only warning, with a Friday night study hall following the second unexcused absence. Their idea would still hold students accountable for missing class while giving them an opportunity to learn from their mistake before facing their punishment. Although the policy is designed to make skipping harder, its success may depend on whether students feel the consequences are fair. As the year continues, the school will have to see if a stricter punishment will actually change student behavior or simply create a new set of concerns.

articles.title: New Policy on Cellphones
paras: After a brutal math class where it seems as though the teacher is speaking another language and a cold science class out in the marsh by Alfond, all students want to do is relax in the dining hall with their friends and check their phones for texts, emails, fantasy football scores, or social media. Or, can we use them appropriately to relax while still connecting with the community?
articles.text: After a brutal math class where it seems as though the teacher is speaking another language and a cold science class out in the marsh by Alfond, all students want to do is relax in the dining hall with their friends and check their phones for texts, emails, fantasy football scores, or social media. However, students must remind themselves that phones can't be visible in the dining hall. Do cell phones make our generation more “brainrotted” and worse at creating conversations? Or, can we use them appropriately to relax while still connecting with the community? This school year, students are prohibited from having their phone visible in the dining hall from 11 am to 1 pm. Mr. Delay said that "Having no phones allows for social interaction and more personal conversation.” While there's no doubt that this is true and lunch is an amazing opportunity for making a friend, so much of what we do in this generation is on our phones and it doesn't stop people from making conversation or meeting a new classmate. Connecting with others can involve taking a phone out to get someone's snapchat or instagram. Ty Harrington ‘29 argues that “Simply talking about stuff on your phone could be a conversation starter.” The idea of no phones during this time isn't an unbearable burden to students, but they would still like to check it for quick reassurance so that they aren't missing out on what's going on in the world or with their friends and family. We're nervous of our phones getting taken away when we simply want to check the time. Cole Travaglini ‘29 says “What if I need to see if a teacher has changed a meeting time?” Cole Cournoyer ‘28 argues that phones don't need to be fully allowed but a simple glance, text, email, or quick check should be allowed. “But sitting there scrolling, not interacting with people should not be allowed.” My simple, and easy solution is that phones should only be used for a quick check or a glance for the time while we are eating lunch. Perhaps teachers could ease up slightly on the taking of cell phones in the dining hall. But students who are sitting there and not interacting with peers should be reminded to put it away. Let's embrace what's a part of our generation, while also being present in our beautiful community.

After a brutal math class where it seems as though the teacher is speaking another language and a cold science class out in the marsh by Alfond, all students want to do is relax in the dining hall with their friends and check their phones for texts, emails, fantasy football scores, or social media. However, students must remind themselves that phones can't be visible in the dining hall. Do cell phones make our generation more “brainrotted” and worse at creating conversations? Or, can we use them appropriately to relax while still connecting with the community?

This school year, students are prohibited from having their phone visible in the dining hall from 11 am to 1 pm. Mr. Delay said that "Having no phones allows for social interaction and more personal conversation.” While there's no doubt that this is true and lunch is an amazing opportunity for making a friend, so much of what we do in this generation is on our phones and it doesn't stop people from making conversation or meeting a new classmate. Connecting with others can involve taking a phone out to get someone's snapchat or instagram. Ty Harrington ‘29 argues that “Simply talking about stuff on your phone could be a conversation starter.”

The idea of no phones during this time isn't an unbearable burden to students, but they would still like to check it for quick reassurance so that they aren't missing out on what's going on in the world or with their friends and family. We're nervous of our phones getting taken away when we simply want to check the time. Cole Travaglini ‘29 says “What if I need to see if a teacher has changed a meeting time?”

Cole Cournoyer ‘28 argues that phones don't need to be fully allowed but a simple glance, text, email, or quick check should be allowed. “But sitting there scrolling, not interacting with people should not be allowed.”

My simple, and easy solution is that phones should only be used for a quick check or a glance for the time while we are eating lunch. Perhaps teachers could ease up slightly on the taking of cell phones in the dining hall. But students who are sitting there and not interacting with peers should be reminded to put it away. Let's embrace what's a part of our generation, while also being present in our beautiful community.

articles.title: Teachers & Their Summer Breaks
paras: Many students may think that teachers do not live interesting lives during summer break. However, teachers have their own hobbies, trips, and other jobs, and they spend time preparing for the next school year. Mr. Ogden and Mrs. Borgatti both spent their summer breaks both traveling and preparing for the next school year.

Mr. Ogden traveled to Korea and China during the summer, where he met some of his former students and their families, giving him a chance to reconnect with students he had taught in the past. The trip allowed him to experience a whole new part of the world while making strong connections through their shared love of golf.

articles.text: Many students may think that teachers do not live interesting lives during summer break. However, teachers have their own hobbies, trips, and other jobs, and they spend time preparing for the next school year. Mr. Ogden and Mrs. Borgatti both spent their summer breaks both traveling and preparing for the next school year. Mr. Ogden traveled to Korea and China during the summer, where he met some of his former students and their families, giving him a chance to reconnect with students he had taught in the past. The trip allowed him to experience a whole new part of the world while making strong connections through their shared love of golf. He also played golf and participated in a golf tournament with his brother. This was especially meaningful for him because Mr. Ogden’s brother had been dealing with a health problem and had undergone a bilateral lung transplant. For Mr. Ogden, winning a tournament mattered less than simply being able to spend time with his brother. Mr. Ogden said, “I have won tournaments before, and that's always fun. But the real victory, the meaningful win -- being able to spend time together. Lots of players came by after the tournament to congratulate us, and what they all said or suggested was that just being there and being together was a win! And they were happy to be a part of it.” Mrs. Borgatti also spent a lot of her summer doing outdoor activities. She led people on trail rides in Vermont and also spent time mountain biking. The highlight of her summer came when she traveled to Alaska and stayed on the Kenai Peninsula for about ten days. She went fishing and horseback riding, and also came face-to-face with a grizzly bear. She caught fish during the trip and sent some of the fresh fish home. These summer activities connected to what she teaches at Govs. As an Environmental Science teacher, she looks for things in nature that she can later use in her class. For example, she took pictures of sights during her trips to use when she teaches. For her, preparation for her classes does not get a vacation! Ms. Borgatti said that she also worked as a consultant outside of Govs in Vermont. As she suggested, many Govs teachers work jobs and continue to learn during their summers. Mr. Ogden and Mrs. Borgatti show that summer break is not only a time when teachers take a break from school. It is also a time when teachers can recharge, have new experiences, and prepare themselves before returning to school.

paras: Govs campus is home to some unusual pets, including Mrs. McLain’s pig Haru, and Mrs. Borgatti’s litter of puppies. Sixteen years ago, an unusual request to babysit a pig became a large addition to Mr. and Mrs. McLain’s family. Mrs. Borgatti helps to breed dogs and often has a bunch of puppies running around. Both the pig and puppies provide good stories and bring a sense of life to campus.

The special name of Mrs. McLain’s pig comes from, "Haru, the great white ninja of whom the prophecies speak of," a quote from the 1997 martial arts comedy film Beverly Hills Ninja. When her daughter was a senior at Bowdoin, she asked her parents to babysit the pig during March break. The pig came to Byfield for two weeks and was then sent back to college. Not long after, he was back at Govs because, “it's really hard to keep an illegal pig in the dorms at a college.”

He is old now so he is not as active, but Mrs. McLain said, “when he was little he would wander across the turf looking for apples under the wild trees.” He also enjoys the fireplace. It’s much more common to find someone with a dog or two instead of a pig, but Mrs. Borgatti goes beyond the expected; instead of one or two dogs, she has raised nine puppies. Mrs. Borgatti works with a breeder and takes care of litters of puppies that will grow up to be in working homes in search and rescue, medical alert, therapy, and hunting careers. She said “It’s a good thing they are cute, because they are high maintenance.” She needs to sleep near the pups for the first couple weeks so they don't wander off or get cold during the night. Puppies can't see or hear for the first 14 days, and she also has to make sure they get enough calcium while they are young. As they grow older, the puppies need to be fed every 2-3 hours to ensure their growth, making it hard for Mrs. Borgatti to be gone for too long. Mrs. Borgatti shared a story of a pup who kept roaming freely around the house and mysteriously escaped her “gated community” frequently. She was confused how she got free while the others were still in the gated area. Mrs. Borgatti happened to come home right when the puppy was scaling the fence to escape while all the other puppies just watched. These pets provide a sense of home to the school community. Though the boarders have to leave their pets to come to Govs, they can still have connections to animals on campus.

articles.title: The New and Improved Weight Room
paras: If you’ve been to the weight room this year, you might notice it looks very different from previous years. Over the summer, the weight room has undergone some changes, both to the room itself and to the programs that take place. Leading these changes is the new Strength and Conditioning coach, Ms. O’Connell, known as Coach KK, class of 2021.

One of the biggest changes to the weight room has been the new equipment and layout. The bottom floor of the weight room has been rearranged and now contains all the squat racks and lifting equipment, while the second floor contains treadmills and bikes. In an interview with Coach KK, she said: “This makes the weight room more functional and can have a better flow when there are large groups of people.” In addition, the weight room has added a lot of new equipment, such as three new trap bars, barbells from Merrimack College, resistance bands, and minibands.

Another big change is the new and improved strength and conditioning afternoon program. Unlike previous years, when the program was just open gym time, this year it is more structured. Athletes in the program train together, split into two groups—intro and advanced—with three lifting sessions a week and two speed and agility sessions. Coach KK said, “Having structured programming that allows students to progress throughout the 9-10 weeks can make them stronger and better prepared for their upcoming seasons.” This afternoon program is open to all sophomores, juniors, and seniors. Coach KK has also been helping varsity teams with team lifts. In an interview with girls varsity soccer captain Hannah Babo ‘27, she described mobility work and four sets of different exercises. The time in the weight room is only thirty minutes; however, Hannah said, “It will help us get faster and get stronger, and it's a very quick 30 minutes. It's very efficient, and Coach KK definitely helps us get better.” Another priority in the weight room is keeping the space clean and well maintained. In past years, the weight room has been left a mess; however, Coach KK plans on enforcing expectations by “holding people accountable who don’t follow the rules.” Additionally, Coach KK said, “If we don't clean up our space, then we can’t use the weight room — but reminders do go a long way.” Over the summer, Coach KK has put a substantial amount of time and effort into changing the weight room and creating a new strength program. Her goal for the year is to “have everyone have a chance to learn a little bit more about exercising and find time to enjoy it.”

articles.text: If you walked into the Remis Art Gallery in Wilkie on Friday, September 18th, you would be greeted by many members of the Govs community coming together to appreciate art submissions from staff across campus. Dr. O’s beautiful violin music fills the room, and you see an assortment of amazing art from staff across campus. Photography, paintings, sculptures, and even embroidery pieces cover the walls and stand on tables around the room. The Staff Art Show gave us a unique opportunity to see the different talents of many Govs staff members. The teachers in the art department, as well as the Kaiser proctors, worked to provide a platform for anyone on the staff to show off their creativity. Kaiser proctor Lana Hardin ‘27 said she believed the event was worthwhile: “I think it really represents how tight of a community we have here at Govs.” Ms. Fitz, another organizer of the art show, said: “It was great to see everyone coming to appreciate what all the artists created.” She hopes to have more staff featured in the future. From Ms. Roberto’s expressive charcoal portraits to Mr. Ogden’s reluctantly submitted poems, the show featured a wide variety of creations and creators. The art show gave the students a chance to see things the staff do outside of work. One thing that really grabbed my interest was Mr. Woodruff’s (head of facilities) handmade skateboards. He made wooden skateboards with each of his kids: one with blue wheels and dark brown wood stripes, and another with green wheels and pink-hued wood stripes down the front. Another piece that stood out to me was Ms. Docks’ quilt. It had thirty squares, each sewn with a different woodland animal and fabric. My personal favorite animals were the beavers, whose teeth were very cute, but there were many others, including bears, foxes, raccoons, and deer. The square in the center said “Docks” and was stitched over a few colorful mushrooms. It was a great night to showcase the true talent of employees from around campus. The Staff Art Show was an amazing chance for the Govs community to see a different side of the people who make this place what it is. With so many unique talents on display, the evening was a great reminder that there is always more to know about the people around us.

articles.title: Three Activity Controversy: Is the Rule Outdated?

When this rule was introduced, out-of-school commitments weren’t as common, especially before COVID: “It [COVID] definitely changed the dynamic of athletes regularly doing three sports, as it was much more common to see that, unlike today,” she said. I also asked Mrs. Barcomb about whether she would change this rule. She said, “With the right support and figuring out what to do with kids while they have a season off, this could be a possibility in the future for maybe seniors to only have to do two seasons.” Her biggest concern was for underclassmen boarding students having nothing to do once the school day concluded. She said it “defeats the purpose of the structure that boarding schools are supposed to have.” Boarding student Porter LaLime ‘27, a football and baseball player, said, “I understand the idea of it, but most people would agree that they want a season off.” Porter felt that giving students more options would be useful. articles.title: When Govs Comes Back to Life
paras: If you ask me, spring at Govs is undefeated. All reasons to stay outside just a little longer before heading home or to the dorms.

articles.title: Do We Have a Cell Phone Policy?
paras: This past year, all public schools across the state were mandated to prohibit cell phone use during school hours. Despite not having to follow this law, in September, Govs made one thing clear: Cell phone use would no longer dominate life on campus.

Despite not having to follow this law, in September, Govs made one thing clear: Cell phone use would no longer dominate life on campus. When we returned to school, cell phone use was the biggest topic of emphasis. Students were met with technology guidelines, a cell phone policy focus group, and a series of announcements reminding us to be present, put away distractions, and build relationships with people instead of devices. At first, there was a noticeable shift in cell phone usage in spaces like the dining hall, Wilkie, and the chapel. Students no longer reverted to cell phones when entering these spaces, and the “encourage, not enforce” approach seemed to work. A few months later, phones have gradually reappeared during lunch and the awkward time before announcements start at morning meeting. Now “no phones in the dining hall” has become more of a joke than a real expectation, leading to the question: if the phone policy isn’t enforced, does it really exist? From a faculty perspective, the phone policy was initially meant to “inspire, not require” to create healthy habits. The school hoped that this approach would make students voluntarily give up phones rather than being forced to comply with a rule. In an email sent to families, Dr. Quimby noted that the policy was designed to encourage presence and be emotionally engaged with our relationships on campus–“protecting and honoring the things that make Govs special.” Another email sent out by Ms. Davey said that “Faculty and staff are empowered to uphold these expectations,” encouraging faculty to remind students to put their phones away in classes and all school spaces. To further limit phone use, Parents were told to communicate with students only outside of school hours. As a student, the reality of instituting a phone policy without clear enforcement has no real effect. The lack of reminders has become inconsistent, making the phone policy seem almost optional. At the start of the school year, almost all teachers required phones to be turned in at the start of class. In most of my classes, the number of phones turned in has dwindled to zero. In the end, the phone policy at Govs raises an important question about school rules and responsibility. While the intention was clear, the phone policy has become largely symbolic, reminding us that truly changing how we use phones on campus requires commitment from the entire community. If the school truly wants to see change in how students use their phones, there needs to be either clear and consistent reminders or a group effort from students choosing to be present on their own.

articles.title: The Ace of Byfield
paras: Every year, the seniors at The Governor’s Academy take a trip to Fenway Park to watch a Red Sox game. It’s a big tradition but last year the energy in the Govs section was different; they weren’t just there to see the worst team in the MLB, the Boston Red Sox. They were there to see one of their own in the visitor’s bullpen in a Chicago White Sox uniform: Shane Smith ‘17. In the heat of the warmups Smith took a moment to toss a baseball to a Govs student, a small gesture that shows the character of the man who has become a campus legend.

In the heat of the warmups Smith took a moment to toss a baseball to a Govs student, a small gesture that shows the character of the man who has become a campus legend. Before he was an MLB All star, Shane Smith was a powerhouse at Govs. He was a three sport varsity captain in football, basketball, and baseball. According to his former baseball coach, Mr. Kinnealey, Shane’s success was never just about raw talent. It was about a blue collar work ethic that set the tone for everyone around him. “Shane was an eye contact, handshake, hard work guy,” Mr Kinnealey recalls. “He was the kid who would carry the equipment bag as a senior.” Mr Kinnealey shared a story that shows Smith’s competitive spirit. During a game against St Sebastian’s, the opposing dugout was “chirping” at Smith while he was on the mound. Most players would lose their cool, but Smith just looked over at the Govs dugout and smiled at his coaches. He let his arm do the talking, shutting them down and proving that he thrived under pressure. It’s the “quiet confidence” that Mr Kinnealey believes allowed Smith to navigate the grind of the minor leagues after going undrafted and recovering from Tommy John Surgery. One of the most inspiring parts of Smith’s journey is how he gave back to Govs during his rise to the pros. While he was playing in Triple A, Smith made a return to campus to help coach our Thirds Basketball team. I was on that team and I saw firsthand that he didn’t treat it like a hobby. He pushed us to be better athletes. He showed us how to condition properly and gave us a great work ethic. As a result of that we had the best season thirds basketball has ever had with six wins and seven losses. Smith returned earlier this year to speak to the student body, and a lot of the athletes were eager to hear from the guy who sat in the same classrooms they do now. Now, when I turn on my xbox to play MLB The Show 26 and throw a no hitter against the future academy president Janciel Martinez using Smith’s 95 MPH heater, I find myself yelling “that’s my coach!” Shane Smith is more than just a pitcher; he is proof that hard work and humility can take you wherever you want to go.

articles.title: The Paradox of Ms. Anderson

Ms. Anderson’s suggestion for students approaching her classes is simple: pay attention. She doesn’t think her classes are as hard as their reputation suggests—if students stay consistently engaged during class time. When asked to describe herself in her own words, Ms. Anderson landed on “kind and approachable”—then laughed at the contrast. “It’s mean content,” she said. “It’s a mean class.” Kind teacher, mean class: that, perhaps, is the Ms. Anderson paradox. Behind every equation derived step by step on the whiteboard, behind every answer to a student’s question about a disappearing negative sign, there is a teacher who chose one of the hardest subjects Govs offers—and decided to make it feel like one of the friendliest.

The beginning of Mr. Hunt’s wrestling program wasn’t just sunshine and rainbows, though. He went winless in his first and second years, and only won one match in his third year. His inspiration to become a high school wrestling coach came from his first wrestling coach, who “never gave up on him in the beginning of his career,” and from his desire to bring that belief to the next generation of wrestlers. Mr. Hunt was not an easy coach, though. He pushed the team to the best of our abilities in the conditioning and live sessions, because he “wants his wrestlers to learn how to face hardship in their life.” I remember being drained from sprints one day and hearing him say, “You feel tired now, but in ten minutes you will feel better. Life is hard.” As a wrestler on the team, one of my most memorable moments happened this year in a trio meet with BB&N and Middlesex. During my second match with Middlesex, I faced a kid who was stronger than me. When the first period ended, I was exhausted and down 3 – 0. Mr. Hunt yelled at me, “Go top! Think of a breakdown to a pin.” As the whistle blew, I drove my opponent into the mat and pinned him. As I walked back to our bench, Mr. Hunt tapped my shoulder and said, “It’s tiring, right? But doesn’t it feel good? I know that kid is bigger than you, but he doesn’t have what you have.” I don’t remember the rest of the day, but his words stuck with me ever since. Tim Duncan, the basketball Hall of Famer once said, “you know it’s time to go when the young guys are doing things you used to do.” That was Mr. Hunt’s explanation for stepping down as the head coach. He told me it is one of his responsibilities to know when to pass the torch to the next guy, and he felt “his time has come.” Thank you, Mr. Hunt, for your years of dedicated hard work for the Governor’s wrestling program.

articles.title: Senior Spring Freedoms
paras: One of the biggest complaints you’ll hear on campus at Govs is that reach is annoying or that the leave policy is overbearing. For most students, the idea of being able to leave campus with their friends to grab a coffee or a quick snack is unrealistic. Because Govs is a closed campus, students are stuck here from Monday to Friday almost every week, until senior spring.

Every spring, seniors are allowed to come and go from campus during their free blocks. After three and a half years of being trapped on campus, students are finally able to experience the freedom of an open campus. So, how much do seniors really utilize this month of freedom before graduation?

For most students, the idea of being able to leave campus with their friends to grab a coffee or a quick snack is unrealistic. Because Govs is a closed campus, students are stuck here from Monday to Friday almost every week, until senior spring. Every spring, seniors are allowed to come and go from campus during their free blocks. After three and a half years of being trapped on campus, students are finally able to experience the freedom of an open campus. So, how much do seniors really utilize this month of freedom before graduation? To find out more, I sent a survey to the senior class. The results showed that 85.7% of seniors plan on taking advantage of these newly gained privileges. Only a slim 14.3% of people said they did not plan to use their senior leave privileges. For those who did plan on leaving campus during their free blocks or PA, there was variation in how often. 43% of seniors said they plan on using leave privileges every day. 38% said they planned on leaving campus 3 to 4 times a week. The remaining 17% of students said they only planned to leave 1 to 2 times per week. The majority of students who said they planned on using senior leaves plan on leaving quite often. This is most likely a result of such a strict policy during the first three and a half years as students at Govs. After living on a closed campus, when students are finally given senior privileges, they are more inclined to leave rather than stay. As seniors make up for their lost freedoms in previous years, they visit several popular destinations in the greater Newburyport area. The top three destinations include Starbucks, Aroma Joe’s, and downtown Newburyport as a whole. Other popular places included Chipotle, Plum Island, Dunkin, or even home. Even if it’s just a short trip to grab a coffee, senior leaves mean that seniors spend less time on campus interacting with the rest of the Govs community. For better food or a change of scenery, as seniors utilize their leave privileges, their presence on campus decreases. This subtle shift marks the beginning of underclassmen stepping up and the end of four years for graduating seniors. Ultimately, senior leave privileges do more than just give students new freedoms. They help transition underclassmen into the next school year and reveal how four years of restricted leave policies shape the community.

paras: One of the most unique parts of The Governor’s Academy is the PA block. It’s a two-hour period from 11:00 to 1:00 that gives students who don’t play in the ensembles a much-needed break in the middle of their day. During this time, students can grab lunch, catch up on homework, or take part in activities that they might not otherwise have time for in their regular schedule. Compared to a typical study hall, PA Block feels more relaxed and flexible, reducing stress and giving students more control over how they spend their time.

It’s a two-hour period from 11:00 to 1:00 that gives students who don’t play in the ensembles a much-needed break in the middle of their day. During this time, students can grab lunch, catch up on homework, or take part in activities that they might not otherwise have time for in their regular schedule. Compared to a typical study hall, PA Block feels more relaxed and flexible, reducing stress and giving students more control over how they spend their time. One of the biggest benefits of PA Block is the opportunity to eat lunch without feeling rushed. Many other schools have lunch blocks that don’t overlap, making it impossible to see friends outside of structured blocks. In the Phillips Dining Hall, students can sit with friends, take a break from classes, and go back for seconds to recharge before the rest of the day. Having that extra time makes lunch feel more relaxed and social, where students can actually unwind, talk, and take a mental break. It also provides time to get homework done during the productive midday hours. Many students finish a good chunk of their work during these hours, allowing them more time to relax in the evening. Students can choose a comfortable space that works best for them, whether in the library, the student center, or in their dorm rooms. Another great part of PA Block is that it allows students to explore interests like art or other creative classes that may not fit into their daily schedules. PA helped me find my love for ceramics when it would otherwise not have fit into my schedule. This class meets twice a week during the PA block and has helped me develop an artistic outlet that was nonexistent until I was 17. Others sing in the choirs or play their instruments in the orchestra and jazz band during this time. This adds variety to the school day and gives students a chance to try something new. Overall, PA Block is both productive and relaxing. Some of my favorite memories of PA block are going on senior leave and walking around Newburyport, playing spikeball on Ingham lawn, discussing in immense detail the ingredients of Lisa’s seven-layer bars, and annoying Chris about a package that was supposed to be delivered weeks ago. PA block sparks new loves, relieves stress, and builds bonds here at The Governors Academy.

articles.text: It is a recent tradition that Govs’ spring play is student written and directed. However, this year is the first where we have had two plays happening in the same season, both being student written! Marilyn Xie ‘26 and Lucy Shows ‘28 have put in a tremendous amount of work to bring their creative visions to life. They brainstormed scenarios, wrote and revised their scripts, and taught the actors how to speak their lines and move their bodies! I interviewed Lucy, the writer/director of the play I’m in (which will be performed May 9th and 13th in the Duncan Philips Library). Lucy’s play, The Ex-Plot, can be described as a drama-comedy based in a small boarding school where a group of students who hardly know one another must work together after false accusations threaten to get them expelled. What follows are some of her insights into the process and what comes next. Q: What was your process of writing this play? LS: I wrote this play for English class, designing it around layered characters inspired by people in my own life. Q: What did you learn through writing it? LS: Writing this play, I learned how difficult it is to write realistic dialogue and decisions. I had to let the plot be driven by the characters rather than vice versa. Q: What was the most challenging part of the writing/directing process? LS: Directing the play was kind of sprung on me. With more time, I would like to be able to modify the more last-minute comedic elements and have more of a set and technical elements. Q: How do you think you’ll do directing a play? LS: Directing is a new challenge for me, but I find that as I step into the role, giving notes and thinking about direction for the cast becomes easier and less awkward. It’s difficult to be a younger director than my actors, but it’s a fun challenge! Q: If you could tell all of Govs anything to get them excited about the play, what would you say? LS: I would say that the play is a mysterious, honest, and sometimes larger-than-life piece centered around the private school experience. Audiences are likely to be familiar with many of the archetypes and should look forward to the unique stage we have in the Duncan Phillips Library.

articles.title: Reviving the Weekends: Bringing Energy Back to Govs
paras: Over four years at Govs, weekend events have had a pretty underwhelming reputation, with many either having little to no guests show up or mainly attracting underclassmen. But why is that? Many different faculty members whose jobs are to plan weekend events have come and gone, so each year has been different from the last.

The off-campus trips, to places like the Topsfield Fair or Boston, have remained a constant over the past three years. The on-campus events, however, have changed a lot. The Academy’s strategic plan lays out a vision for the future of the campus and includes some major changes. According to Paul Nardone, Head of the Board of Trustees, the plan is to build three brand new buildings: an athletic and wellness facility, a new dorm, and a new academic building. This plan seeks to update many of the facilities on Govs campus while also preserving the older feel. The athletic and wellness facility is in the most exciting news. Currently, the Alumni Memorial Gymnasium consists of an: exercise room with limited weight racks, few machines, and a small size that easily becomes overcrowded; a field house with three basketball courts surrounded by an indoor track that isn’t fit to hold meets; and many outdated locker rooms. A more modern facility would be a game changer not just for varsity athletes but the whole Govs community as a whole. The dormitories fit the look of the oldest boarding school in America, but with age comes outdated living facilities. Living in Ingham Dormitory, I can say there’s definitely a lot of interior and exterior work needed. For everyone who lives on campus, the dorm is considered our home and has the power to affect our daily lives. From newer bathrooms to improved common rooms where students can bond together, the addition of modern dorms can change the living experience entirely for boarders. Then there is the new academic building. When I sit in a classroom in Frost, I feel a sense of pride but also isolation from the present day. The Board of Trustees plans to combine a traditional feel with a more up to date approach to classroom design. A modern classroom could change the way students learn and teachers teach. A lot of other prep schools we compete with have these newer learning environments, so this feels like a much needed change. Nardone made it clear that the Board of Trustees is committed to upgrading Govs campus while also maintaining the history that comes along with it. He says, “Our Board of Trustees remains focused on continuing to invest in maintaining and upgrading our campus infrastructure over the next five years.” This matters because there are many older buildings that need some love and should not be neglected with newer buildings being built. The bottom line is that the strategic plan is a pretty big deal. Most of us won’t be at Govs to see it come to life, but for future students this change could shape what it means to go to Govs.

She balanced this work with teaching, developing a depth of knowledge that students and faculty regularly rely on. Reflecting on the many times she’s been called to help, she joked, “For some reason people think I won’t be nervous, so they call me!” Her rescues on campus include what was believed to be a bat, but turned out to be a flying squirrel. Other calls involved actual bats in dorms and showers, all of which she safely rescued. In one case, she helped an injured beaver on the side of the road. “Its hip was dislocated and I was able to pop it back in,” she said. The beaver was later rehabilitated and released back into the wild. Her journey into breeding dogs began unexpectedly. Through her dedication, compassion, and energy, she has created something lasting within the Govs community. Change can sometimes be a good thing by shifting movement and goals, but it can also be difficult for players who are just trying to develop fundamentals and succeed together. Every coach has a different approach to the game. One may be all about discipline and structure, while another may prioritize freedom and creativity. While both philosophies can be successful, it is difficult to have to switch back and forth between them. For the 2024 season the coach was James Cramphin, whose coaching style consisted of well disciplined fundamentals and strong habits that created consistent results. He was replaced in 2025 by James Baker, who focused primarily on pitching fundamentals and breaking down every little piece of movement. The 2026 season brings Carson Cross. He was drafted in 2015 by the St. Louis Cardinals and played for UNH for four years before that as a stand out pitcher. His coaching style has not yet been displayed but the team is eager to hit the field with him in Florida to create the bond Govs baseball has always been about. Another aspect of the game that has been impacted is team chemistry. It takes time for a good baseball team to build a level of trust between the players and the coaches and learn each other’s habits and tendencies. When a coach resigns after only one year, all of that trust goes out the window for the falling year. The players then have to work to build that trust with a new coach. For younger players, it can be difficult to know what to expect from year to year and who will be leading the team. However, this has forced the players to build resilience and mental toughness. We have had to adapt quickly, communicate more effectively, and remain focused on the game under uncertain conditions. The captains and upperclassmen have had to take on an even bigger role to keep the team together during this time of transition. In a way, the players–not the coaches– have become the backbone of the program. This year, the veteran players must work to build the team chemistry and to carry forward the best practices of past coaches. Looking ahead, many of the athletes hope for greater consistency so that the team can develop and establish an identity. Consistency in coaching would enable the players to learn and develop over several years of a particular coaching system, which would help establish a sense of tradition.

Over the past few years, a question has arisen about the winter exam schedule: Should it be moved back to before winter break? Mid-term exams were originally scheduled before the break. During the 2020–2021 school year, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic with partially online learning, the school chose not to administer traditional exams. When exams were reinstated in the 2022–2023 school year, the school used that opportunity to reconsider December exams. Mr. Satow said, “One of the big factors was to honor the semester-long classes. It was awkward for them to be giving their semester exam three weeks before the end of the semester.” Most of the semester-long classes are English, History, and Art courses, and giving a “final” exam before the course had actually concluded was inconsistent and unfair to teachers. Moving exams to the true end of the semester allowed those classes to fully complete their content before assessing students. At the same time, the school shifted from large, subject-based exams in the field house to block-based assessments in the classrooms. Changing this gave teachers more flexibility to use projects, presentations, and alternative formats instead of only long sit-down tests. When this change was originally made, it was discussed among just the faculty. Student voices were not taken into consideration, although most of us don’t want to take exams in the first place. After sending out a poll, two-thirds of the students who responded want exams to be before the break. When I asked Andrew Melly ‘26 what it’s like coming from a school that had exams before break, he said, “There’s nothing to stress about over break, and you can only relax. Here at Govs, you have the stress of exams hanging over your head while you’re on break.” Ultimately, when deciding on an exam schedule, not everyone will agree. There is an equal argument from both sides. Having exams after the break may accommodate semester-long courses, but does that make our break less enjoyable and more stressful? When finishing my interview with Mr. Satow, he said, “We’d always be willing to hear people’s opinions. If we’re not listening to new ideas, then we’re not really doing our jobs.” Discussion among our peers allows teachers and students to better understand each other’s perspectives and work toward a schedule that best supports the school community.

articles.title: Too Many Day Students
paras: When people hear “boarding school,” they usually picture a campus where everyone lives full-time and the school feels separate from the outside world. Govs isn’t like that. About 60% of students are boarders and 40% are day students, which makes it different from a lot of traditional boarding schools. On top of that, many of the boarders live within two hours of campus. So even though they live at school, students are still pretty connected to home, which changes the overall feel of campus.

About 60% of students are boarders and 40% are day students, which makes it different from a lot of traditional boarding schools. On top of that, many of the boarders live within two hours of campus. So even though they live at school, students are still pretty connected to home, which changes the overall feel of campus. I have gone to both Govs and Brewster, a school with 95% boarding and 5% day students, so I have seen the contrast firsthand. At Brewster, everyone stays on campus every weekend due to the fact that no one lives within two hours of campus, and most are a flight away. At Brewster, there is more buy-in from people for campus activities. Everyone attends every Saturday game, every school dance, and every weekend activity because frankly, there is nothing better to do. With this buy-in from the community, the events are more fun and competitive. At Govs, the dean’s team works hard to put on fun events, dances, and games, but due having many on campus leave Friday through Sunday, this makes the events have less energy. The mix between boarding and day students makes the social life feel more balanced, however. We get to have more of a normal high school experience, whether it is going into Boston for dinner, or watching a local football game. It’s pretty common for a boarder at Govs to get invited to a day student’s house for dinner or even to stay for a weekend. During hockey tournaments or even unexpected events like power outages, boarders often stay with day families or other boarders who live close by. That creates connections that go beyond just campus life. At Brewster, there were definitely kids from New England, but most students were from all over the country, which made it so cliques didn’t really form as much and people were more mixed together. At the Governor’s Academy, a lot of students, even boarders, are from Massachusetts or nearby, so people sometimes come in already knowing each other. That can lead to more defined friend groups early on. At the same time, this local presence adds its own kind of diversity, especially in perspectives and backgrounds within the region. Govs feels different because of that mix. The 60/40 split between boarding and day students gives it a unique identity. It still feels like a boarding school, but not in a super isolated way. Overall, even if Brewster felt tighter as one whole community, Govs creates really strong bonds within smaller friend groups. It ends up being a good balance between independence and having a close, tight-knit group around you.

Through this, I learned that Govs has always toed the line of neutrality. There have been a few exceptions to our school’s political isolation, though only in times of national crisis like the two World Wars. During both of those, less athletic afternoon programs were cancelled so that students could become more physically fit and ready to serve their country. However, this has never been done since then, and given social norms and widespread antiwar beliefs in our modern era, it seems this will never happen again. So, the question remains: Should we “pop” the Byfield bubble? As national politics become more divisive, it becomes harder to openly discuss them with friends for fear of getting pushed away due to differing opinions. Our PPD meetings in the fall and winter of 2024 didn’t always relate directly to national politics, but they gave us licence to discuss important issues. It was for that reason I was happy to see another PPD meeting early this school year on freedom of speech. From what I saw, it seemed like mostly everyone agreed on that issue. However, we haven’t had another meeting since then, even though political strife has continued outside of our bubble. In a midterm year like this one, especially with current political issues, it would be productive to bring back PPD. Besides allowing students to talk about politics, this will encourage them to keep involved in and educated about elections, whether local, statewide, or national. After all, if a school’s purpose is to prepare its students for life as adults, it is important that students are taught the importance of fulfilling their civic duty of voting. Only about 45% of the world’s population has that opportunity, so we need to make it count!

To know more about Congress, it’s hard to find a more effective way than being a Congressman yourself. Luckily, Harvard Model Congress, also known as HMC, provides an optimal platform. Organized entirely by Harvard students and staff, HMC is held annually for four days in Boston, welcoming high school students domestically and internationally. HMC requires students to assume the role of real-life congressmen, senators, and members of government. Students are required to step into their represented politicians’ shoes even if their personal political views don’t align with those of their politicians. As a delegate in the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence this year, I deeply felt the emphasis on representing the politician at HMC. For example, my politician, Senator Roger Wicker from Mississippi, leans toward installing more military infrastructure locally to strengthen the US’s control in Africa. Although I personally believed this to be too aggressive, I still spoke in favor of this idea and negotiated with others around it. I also remember arguing against other delegates over whether the government should partner with tech companies to fight foreign cyberattacks. With an equal representation for both parties, the bills that were passed were usually highly bipartisan in my committee. “People are just nice in person” is what I felt the most in my committee. While some heated debate indeed took place when in session, delegates from my committees were very friendly privately. We talked playfully about the HMCcrushes Instagram account, complained about the disappointing aspects of our school, and cheered each other’s dreams. We also got to ask random questions to our Harvard Undergraduate Committee chairs about the craziest things they had done at Harvard, their SAT/ACT scores, whether they were happier after entering Harvard, and their definition of success. It only took a day or two to get along with most of the people. Here are some insights from Mr. Satow, who is the new director of HMC, about what he is looking for from applicants: Are you going to be engaged in representing your politician and follow Parliamentary Procedure (don’t worry, no test about this in the application!) Are you going to be comfortable raising your hands in a room full of strangers? Yes, this leans toward extroverted people. If you are more introverted, are you still willing to be active in smaller groups, such as the National Security Council and the President’s Cabinet? My placard, signed by my committee’s delegates and chairs, stands still on my desk in my room, motivating me constantly. Joining HMC is a decision I’ve never regretted. Apply and put your own placard on the table, future delegates!

But is automatic censure a good thing? Does this rule really prevent students from getting out of line? I would argue no. I interviewed seniors from other prep schools to see if they had any system like this. One responded, “What? Is that a real thing?” Even without senior spring censure, these other schools still manage without mass outbreaks of delinquency. At a time when seniors are supposed to be preparing for complete independence and the college experience, the threat of one mistake potentially ruining your future is problematic. Senior privileges should reflect the trust we’ve built over these four years. Increased levels of freedom would, in my opinion, make students less likely to rebel because they feel appreciative of the trust being placed in them and wouldn’t want to break it. I’m not saying that consequences shouldn’t exist; in fact that’s integral to growth. However, this pseudo-censure operates on the notion that if left unchecked, seniors will push the rules until the breaking point. I would argue that, if anything, senior spring is when students are most aware of what they have to lose. After four years of work, all culminating in getting a diploma, I think very few would be willing to jeopardize that, censure or no. I propose getting rid of the censure policy because if we are ready to be fully independent adults in August, we deserve the benefit of the doubt in March.

articles.title: Why Are AP Classes Being Eliminated?
paras: Govs is eliminating Advanced Placement classes in the next two years, a decision that will change how students approach rigorous work. Long seen as the highest academic challenge and a way for seniors to show colleges that they are ready for college-level work, AP courses follow a strict nationwide curriculum created by the College Board to prepare students for standardized exams each May.

Mrs. Gold from the Academic Office said the decision to remove AP classes altogether is intended to give departments and teachers more flexibility in designing challenging courses. Long seen as the highest academic challenge and a way for seniors to show colleges that they are ready for college-level work, AP courses follow a strict nationwide curriculum created by the College Board to prepare students for standardized exams each May. Mrs. Gold from the Academic Office said the decision to remove AP classes altogether is intended to give departments and teachers more flexibility in designing challenging courses. Instead of following the strict curriculum set by the College Board, teachers will be able to create their own advanced classes that push students “in ways that are not constrained by the pace and content limitations of the AP curriculum.” The highest-level classes will now be “Signature Advanced” courses, which will represent the highest level of study in each department and will “require strong preparation, prerequisites, and teacher recommendations.” According to Mrs. Gold, the goal is not to “dilute the rigor but to elevate it.” She explained that while AP courses provide a clear framework, they are also tied to a prescribed curriculum and a high-stakes May exam, which can pressure teachers to move quickly through material and “teach to the test” instead of spending more time on complex ideas and extended projects. One of the biggest concerns for students about the change is how it will appear on college applications. The academic office says that they will “work closely with the College Counseling Office to communicate the rigor of our Advanced courses in school profiles and counselor letters.” They note that selective colleges evaluate students within the context of their school. When a school does not offer AP courses, students are not penalized; what matters most is that students pursue the most challenging courses available to them and perform well. Departments have discussed the pros and cons of the change, asking, “If we weren’t constrained by the AP curriculum, what other topics could we explore?” Teachers may keep strong AP content while expanding it, and they will be given professional development time to work on these new classes. Govs is not alone in changing its AP policy. Several other independent schools — including Milton Academy, Nobles, St. George’s, Middlesex, Phillips Academy, and Phillips Exeter Academy — have also moved away from AP programs to create more flexible advanced classes. As the transition moves forward, helping families, students, and colleges understand the change will require clear communication and planning. Whether the new approach ultimately benefits students will become clearer in the years to come. For now, the shift represents a significant change in how Govs defines academic rigor, placing more responsibility on departments and teachers to shape what advanced learning will look like for future students.

articles.title: What Truly Keeps Govs Alive
paras: Community is the heartbeat of Govs. An outsider would think that programming keeps this school going, assuming that the fun hockey games or themed lunches keep the spirit alive, but it’s the niche moments that members of the community provide that fill our cups when they are empty. It is easy to get caught up in insignificant things, but if we look outwards we can appreciate the real core of what makes Govs the school that it is. What are the true reasons why students are so comfortable and passionate about their involvement on campus? The answer reveals itself every week on our campus. Take Friday, 2/13, for example. In the afternoon, ceramics students sold handmade pottery to support the First Parish Newbury Food Pantry, and the Valentine’s flower sale filled the dining hall with many smiles. That evening, girl’s basketball played a spirited game against Pingree, and the cast, pit band, and tech crew of the musical Mamma Mia! made the stage come alive. On 2/17, students celebrating the Chinese New Year dined together in Boston. During 2/19 – 2/22, Harvard Model Congress delegates simulated the U.S. Government with their knowledge and wit. In such diversity, community blooms. From stage lights in Bergman Theater to goals scored on the basketball court, from intercultural celebrations to academic pursuits, each community member’s contribution is valued, and their talents and perspectives help the campus remain deeply connected and vibrant. Even beyond campus, this talent still thrives. Govs continues to celebrate alumna Alex Carpenter ‘11 as she represents the country at the 2026 Winter Olympics. Long before she represented the USA on the world’s biggest stage, Carpenter wore cardinal threads and the Governor’s crest. Carpenter’s career at Govs was nothing short of dominant. In just 100 games, she recorded an astonishing 427 points (239 goals and 181 assists), etching herself into the Govs history books as one of the most prolific players in school history. Her scoring ability, vision, and competitive drive elevated the girls’ hockey program and set a new standard for excellence. Carpenter continued her career at Boston College, where she quickly became one of the top players in NCAA women’s hockey and won the Patty Kazmaier Award, given annually to the best player in women’s Division I hockey. Carpenter has made us proud by bringing the Byfield spirit to the larger world. For current Governor’s student athletes, Carpenter’s journey serves as proof that dedication at Govs can lead anywhere, even to Olympic glory.

articles.title: Celebrating Mr. C’s 35 Years at The Academy
paras: When Mr. C arrived at The Governor’s Academy in 1990, he came with a simple goal: to teach and coach high school students. Thirty-five years later, as he prepares to retire, he leaves behind a legacy that has shaped generations of Govs students both in and out of the classroom.

Before Govs, Mr. C taught at the Fay School, a junior boarding school in Southborough. Though he valued his experience there, he wanted to coach and work with older, more mature kids. Through a colleague from the Fay School, he found his way to Govs in 1990 to fulfill his dream.

Through a colleague from the Fay School, he found his way to Govs in 1990 to fulfill his dream. When he arrived at Govs, his coaching career began with the Varsity Boys Hockey team, where he coached for nine years, seven of those as head coach. He then transitioned to coaching the Varsity Girls hockey team. When I asked him what the transition was like, he said, “In some ways, it was a blessing in disguise. It was different than coaching the guys, but for me it was better.” Among his years of coaching, one season that stood out to him was 2007-2008, Alex Carpenter’s freshman year. That year, they had seven forwards and three defenders, about half of the normal size of a hockey team. The short bench didn’t stop them. The team reached the New England Tournament championship game, which went into double overtime. The other team received a penalty, and Govs scored the game-winning goal. Mr. C said, “That memory, that group of kids, that year, and what we did with the size of the team, that was a special group. Some of them were seniors, but Alex and two kids that she played with were in their freshman years, so I got the chance to work with them for three more years.” While at Govs, Mr. C didn’t just coach hockey; he has remained in the History Department throughout his tenure; he has also served as senior class advisor, dorm head in Eames for 29 years, and weekend program coordinator. He coached football during his first nine years and has coached golf since 1997. Yet when asked about the most rewarding part of his career, he reflects on the relationships he has formed while living in the dorm, being a senior class advisor, mentoring students, and fully immersing himself in campus life. His own three sons grew up at Governor’s, making the school not just a workplace, but home. In retirement, Mr. C looks forward to spending time with family, especially as a seventh grandchild arrives this summer. He plans to spend time at his family’s home in New Hampshire, enjoying simple moments outdoors with his children and grandchildren. As he steps away from Governor’s, the community thanks Mr. C for his dedication, mentorship, and steady presence. His impact will continue to be felt long after his final class and final practice. So when you see Mr. C walking around campus, thank him for all he has done for this community.

articles.title: Inside the Legacy of Girls JV Puck
paras: JV Girls hockey is the only sport where you might see someone fall, laugh, get back up, score a goal, and then celebrate like they just won the Olympics. In the middle of that chaos, though, everyone is trying their absolute hardest. That balance is what defines JV Puck.

The program has been running for 30 years, and at its heart is Coach Karin, now in his 28th season coaching the team. Mr. Karin treats his team with the same seriousness and dedication as any varsity team on campus. He wants the best for his players and for them to all grow. According to Coach Karin, “what sets JV apart is how students continue to play when they have other options that don’t require late-night practices,” something that inspires him every day. That choice–to stay committed even when it isn’t the easiest option–speaks to the kind of culture he and the team has built.

That phrase immediately raised a series of questions in my mind. What is gluten? What does it do to our bodies? And most importantly, if something is gluten-free, does that mean the unforgettable flavor I experienced on my first day of school is somehow changed or even lost? Here is what I learned about gluten. Gluten is the main storage protein in wheat, mainly consisting of gliadin and glutenin. Although similar proteins–existing in rye, barley, and oats–are also referred to as gluten, the gluten used in or naturally existing in pizza, bread, pasta, and other baked goods—and the health issues related to gluten—are primarily concentrated on wheat. The crunchy texture of pizza is created by gliadin and glutenin. Gliadins contribute to the viscosity and extensibility of the dough, whereas glutenins give the dough its strength and elasticity. This is why bread rises and forms a bubble structure within it. Therefore, if you enjoy the moisture and crunchy texture of pizza, gluten-free pizza might not be the most optimal choice. Despite the significant role that gluten plays in improving the texture and structure of baked goods, both researchers and the public have shown growing attention about gluten-led health concerns. Gluten is highly associated with several health issues, including coeliac disease, wheat allergy, and non-coeliac gluten sensitivity. Due to the unique structure of gluten, its peptides are resistant to break down, meaning they are difficult for our gut to digest. As a result, some people may have difficulty processing gluten-containing foods, leading to symptoms such as diarrhea, gas, and bloating. Moreover, about one percent of Western populations have an autoimmune disease—coeliac disease—in which patients’ immune systems target gluten proteins in their small intestine, causing chronic damage to the intestine. People who suffer from wheat allergies should also avoid gluten, and gluten has been linked to non-coeliac gluten sensitivity, although the mechanism is still unclear and debatable. We should all appreciate the options that the dining hall offers, providing more food choices for people with different needs. Meanwhile, if you do not experience any of the symptoms mentioned above, there is no reason to be afraid of gluten. So the next time you walk past the pizza station, definitely grab a slice or two and enjoy all of the flavor that our dining hall serves.

According to an alumnus of the pre-COVID days, the schedule “was hard to keep track of.” What we now consider an early start was a sleep in, and the idea of popping into Dhall to grab a snack between classes was unheard of. Before COVID and online/hybrid classes, students attended five classes each day (except Wednesday), each lasting 50 minutes with a five-minute passing period in between. This meant constant shuffling between buildings, and if you arrived even a minute late, class was likely to already be in full swing. This older schedule also lacked the Thursday morning convocation block, which was originally on Tuesday afternoons, depriving students of the occasional much-needed recharge. As a person who has lived both schedules in his time as a student and teacher, Sr. Norton offers a unique view into the subject. As a student, he would have rather had the current schedule, but when asked if as a teacher he thought it would be helpful to meet four times a week, he said, “I do,” and that having shorter classes could be a good thing: “It keeps your guys attention better. Sometimes for an hour you have to drag it a little bit.” The change in schedule was, according to Ms. Block, the chair of the scheduling committee, “In response to COVID.” During quarantine, teachers saw how exhausted students were becoming, and this made them more vulnerable to infection. In our interview Ms Block told me that they wanted to prioritize sleep and restoration, so the 7:45 start time on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Fridays was first to go. Next, since everyone had felt so disconnected during purely online classes, they needed to reintegrate morning meetings and convocations so the school could come together again. The result led us to the schedule we have now, but it wasn’t meant to last forever. After quarantine and the threat of COVID had largely passed, the committee sent out a survey and looked at the schedules for other prep schools around us. In the end, the topics Ms. Block told me they deemed most important were: “consistent start and stop times, an 8:15 start, and 10-minute passing time between classes.” This change to the travel time coincided with the introduction of the Alfond Center. As anyone who’s ever had to make the trek knows, five minutes would make it impossible to get to class on time. A committee has been formed to consider a new schedule for the future. Once again, we will have to face the difficult questions: How often should classes meet? How long should classes be? And, most importantly, how can we make the school better?
