As a senior, you have to submit what feels like a college thesis explaining your goals, timeline, materials, impact, and why you, specifically, deserve to do this project. It’s less “share your idea” and more “defend your life choices.” Hence the Judge Judy comparison; both she and the SSTP committee are no-nonsense arbiters eager to shut down weak excuses and to assert their authority. Here are some student stories: Student: Joe shmoe, ‘67. Proposal: an incredibly detailed engineering project. The perhaps apocryphal story goes that this student’s proposal was labeled “too easy.” Legend holds that Mr. Hunt was dropped from the committee–and reassigned to the student parking committee–after approving this project. If that is true, it raises the obvious question: what exactly counts as challenging? The criteria sometimes feel mysterious, like Mr. Hunt himself. Student: Andrew Melly ‘26. Proposal: to create 25 handmade ceramic mugs for the dining hall. As an AP Ceramics student, I thought it made sense. The dining hall constantly runs out of mugs by PA block, and I figured new ones could brighten people’s mornings and actually serve a purpose. I was interrogated about my ceramics experience and required to present a signed court order to the dining hall staff to prove I was allowed to make mugs. To this day I spend two hours per night on my SSTP proposal instead of working on my college essays. Student: Jack Couture, ‘26. Proposal: to write a cookbook and create a video cooking channel that combined ancient Chinese recipes with his experience in Chinese 1. Jack was told it might not be rigorous enough. He then proposed a second project involving filming his daily hockey stick taping which was approved without much resistance. As the great philosopher once said, “Rigor is in the eye of the beholder.” Senior Spring Term is still a great opportunity. Most of us apply because we genuinely want to create something before we graduate. But the approval process can feel less like encouragement and more like an audition. Maybe that’s just part of the tradition. Or maybe next year we should invite Judge Judy to sit in on the committee meetings. At least judge Judy gives you a reason for your conviction…

articles.title: Want A PhD? Dr. Alex: Love Cake Soup First!
paras: Have you ever wondered what it feels like to be called “Dr.” instead of “Mr.” or “Ms.”? Dr. Alex, the AP Biology teacher at Govs, received her PhD from Case Western Reserve University. She focused on neuroscience and neuropharmacology, specifically on the interaction between serotonin and dopamine, and used laboratory rats for professional experimental procedures. articles.text: Have you ever wondered what it feels like to be called “Dr.” instead of “Mr.” or “Ms.”? Dr. Alex, the AP Biology teacher at Govs, received her PhD from Case Western Reserve University. She focused on neuroscience and neuropharmacology, specifically on the interaction between serotonin and dopamine, and used laboratory rats for professional experimental procedures. I interviewed Dr. Alex and asked about her opinion on whether today’s students should pursue a PhD. As the old saying goes, “All that glitters is not gold.” VL: What was the most challenging part of your PhD experience? KA: In the labs I did in my high school and college, students always knew what reactions they would get, and teachers made sure the lab was going to work. That gave me a false impression of what real science was. When I tried to do a PhD, I almost never got the expected result. 99 out of 100 experiments didn’t show anything at all. During my PhD, we kept a lab journal recording the number of each rat we used in the experiment. I know that the number got up to like 405. VL: How does your PhD experience influence you as a teacher? KA: A lot of high school teachers tell you exactly the method to use, the exact hypothesis to test, and what you expect to get. I try to have students design their own procedure and design their own hypothesis, and then evaluate their hypothesis. It doesn’t matter if you got good data or not. It matters whether you can take the data that you’ve got and interpret what it means and what you would do differently next time. It’s like making a cake. You figure out how to make a cake, like researching what is going to react together to make the cake rise. You may end up getting a cake or getting a cake soup, but I don’t care. I care what you could do differently next time to get closer to that cake. In real science, you never get a cake the first time. VL: How could students know if pursuing a PhD is the right decision to make? KA: Students who might enjoy doing a PhD usually feel amazed when learning something new and appreciate the complexities of the subject. But a PhD is long and arduous, and it could be a really bad choice if your heart isn’t in it. My recommendation to students is always to try to get some research experience in a lab, in college, or in the summer, even if it’s an unpaid internship, so that you know whether it’s something you like or not. Is your heart tilting toward earning a PhD? Dr. Alex mentions that earning a PhD requires curiosity and persistence, but it is also rewarding and offers many job opportunities in pharmaceuticals and private sector industries. A PhD might not be for everyone, but it will never hurt to learn more about the actual experience of it!

articles.title: A Century of Governor’s Academy Dorms
paras: Stepping foot on the campus of The Governor’s Academy and taking a walk through all the dorms is a walk through the school’s history. Over a century of campus housing is built into the walls of dorms like Moody, Farmhouse, and Doggett, and according to Ms. Slater, the school’s historian, “these dorms still shape how students live together today.” After sitting down and learning about the dorms’ rich history, it has become clear that the dorms play a huge role in the kind of community they create.
articles.text: Stepping foot on the campus of The Governor’s Academy and taking a walk through all the dorms is a walk through the school’s history. Over a century of campus housing is built into the walls of dorms like Moody, Farmhouse, and Doggett, and according to Ms. Slater, the school’s historian, “these dorms still shape how students live together today.” After sitting down and learning about the dorms’ rich history, it has become clear that the dorms play a huge role in the kind of community they create. Built in 1914, Moody is one of the oldest dorms on campus. Its small interior gives the dorm a charming and historic feel. Ms. Slater notes that “smaller dorms tend to have tighter communities,” making it easier for students to connect with each other and get a sense of boarding school life. The catch is that it’s “not cost effective to have a bunch of small dorms anymore,” so new facilities tend to mean larger dorms, which makes it hard to recreate that same cozy feel. The common spaces of these dorms also affect how students interact on a day to day basis. Ms. Slater compared a newer dorm like Doggett with older dorms like Ingham and Eames, suggesting the dorms with better common rooms bring students together by encouraging them to “hang out there, watch movies, whatever.” She went on to say “better common rooms encourage people to actually hang out together, and that builds community.” Each dorm’s common room reflects the priorities of the time when they were built, with Doggett presenting the most current thinking. With so many older dorms on campus, the facilities staff have a hard time keeping up with what needs fixing. Ms. Slater mentioned that the older dorms’ electrical systems weren’t designed for modern technology, which was the main reason for limiting refrigerators in rooms. Heating and plumbing are also challenges in trying to modernize these dorms. Ms. Slater explained that if you could look into the walls of an older dorm, you would see decades of electrical and plumbing fixes from past facilities crews. Still, the older dorms come with their own personality that newer dorms can’t replicate. The archives contain a number of artifacts of past dorm traditions: a book of old songs that Moody residents used to write and sing; a cabinet with decades of student signatures from Ambrose House, a former dorm on campus; a paddle from Eames used for activities which would no longer be allowed; and a t-shirt from Ingham, with its notorious “Ingham Country Club” nickname. Many of these traditions have lapsed, but they show that students want to create memories in these dorms, a tradition that lives on today. Even though campus is constantly changing, the past memories are evident in the buildings that remain. The dorms we are living in at this very moment tell a story of how the school maintains centuries of history in its bricks and mortar.

When you step foot into a classroom at Govs, you’ll find 13-year-old “young sheldons,” and reclassed athletes as old as 20, both on non-traditional paths to the same diploma. The timeline to graduation at private schools is drastically different from that at public schools. As a result, classrooms in subjects like languages and math often include students of all grade levels and ages. To understand how age affects the classroom, I interviewed Jack Couture ‘26 and Tabi Kelly ‘29 on their experiences with age in their Chinese class. For Jack, his time at Govs included upperclassmen who mentored him, “completely changing the course of his high school career.” Now, as an upperclassman, he feels a sense of responsibility for his younger classmates and hopes to have a similar impact on them, as older students once did for him. From another lens, age influences classroom participation. Tabi, as a freshman, views age as an advantage for older students in the classroom when it comes to participation. As a younger student, she is more reluctant to participate in classes where upperclassmen are present. She said “older students are more confident and have more experience participating,” allowing them to feel more comfortable answering questions and helping others. Despite recognizing the classroom confidence that comes with age, she says that she does not always feel that pressure in Chinese because everyone is learning and they all make the same mistakes. It has three full courts, allowing for multiple teams to practice at once and for many people to play basketball, tennis, volleyball, or other sports. Additionally, the Alumni Gym is in great shape and continues to be enjoyed by many students at Govs. And finally, the training room is a spacious area that gives athletes room to stretch and receive the help they need if they are injured. However, there are several negatives that some would argue outweigh the positives. For starters, the flooring of the courts is very worn down and hard, leading to many knee, shin, and ankle injuries. In addition, the track in the fieldhouse has become impractical and at times dangerous due to the space not being big enough for many runners at a time and the turns being too sharp. Many students have also complained that the weight room is too small and does not have enough machines or space. Finally, there are a few maintenance issues that require attention, including inadequate lighting in some rooms and roof leaks that result in water dripping onto the track and basketball courts. When deciding which building to renovate next,I believe the fieldhouse should be the first building that should be renovated. We should expand the weight room so that more people can use machines, and we should fix the roof, flooring, and lighting. In addition, we should also improve the track so that it is viable to host track meets. The fieldhouse is a great building on campus, but I believe that it needs to be severely renovated in order to become an even more pivotal part of the Govs community and live up to its true potential.

articles.title: Day Students and the Driving Dilemma
paras: It’s 10:55 AM on a Friday morning. You just had your first two classes of the day, and your next class does not start until 2:15 PM. As you part ways with your boarder friend heading back to their dorm for a three-hour nap, you consider going to the crowded Dining Hall to yell across the table so your friends can hear you, or going to the Student Center to “rot.”

One option that is not available is leaving campus during this time because the Governors Academy has strict rules regarding day student driving privileges. Many day students want more freedom to balance work and happiness. With an open campus, some might be able to go home, while others could just go to Newburyport. Governor’s should reconsider the driving policy to allow day students to be able to leave campus during the school day.

Students often see the issue through the lens of fairness and independence, while faculty prioritize responsibility and risk. Perhaps a new policy could be created that would accommodate all of these priorities, giving teachers peace of mind and day students a break from campus.

From harmless jokes to elaborate plans, seniors use this tradition to celebrate the close of their time on campus. As Ms. Fitzgerald, a longtime faculty member, explains, “I have been here for 40 years, and there have always been pranks.” Over the years, some pranks have become especially memorable, standing out for their creativity or humor. Ms. Fitzgerald recalls examples such as hundreds of carefully placed cups covering the entire lobby of Wilkie, forcing anyone who entered to navigate the space slowly and carefully to avoid spilling them. She also remembers students saran wrapping faculty cars, turning an ordinary parking lot into a scene of confusion and laughter. These pranks exemplify the creativity and humor that define the tradition. The most successful pranks are the ones that surprise the community while remaining harmless. While the tradition of pranks has persisted, the approach has altered. According to Ms. Fitzgerald, “seniors as a whole have become more responsible and less destructive in planning their pranks.” However, she also noted that this can sometimes lead to a lack of creativity, resulting in the repetition of the same prank throughout multiple senior classes. In recent years, for example, many seniors have relied on the same prank of moving backpacks during morning meetings, confusing underclassmen but ultimately creating little lasting impact. This repetition suggests that modern pranks do not always match the originality of earlier efforts. The administration’s response to senior pranks plays a key role in shaping the tradition. Mrs. Fitzgerald alluded to the fact that the school is “usually okay as long as the academic day is not interrupted, the pranks aren’t dangerous or destructive, and it doesn’t require the maintenance team to clean up.” The guidelines create clear boundaries for the students to follow, drawing the line between a successful prank and one that goes too far. She emphasizes that, “the seniors need to be responsible and fix whatever has been disturbed,” encouraging students to think carefully about how their actions affect others and themselves. As this year’s seniors approach graduation, anticipation is already building around what their prank might be. With such a long standing tradition behind them, the pressure is on to create something that is both original and respectful of the school’s expectations. Whichever path they take, it will undoubtedly reflect their legacy as a class and add another chapter to the long story of senior pranks at The Governors Academy.

Be resilient; don’t let failure compound itself to make a bigger failure. Finally, Ms. Allen suggests prioritizing a free block in junior’s schedules. A free block has two benefits: it gives you more time to catch up on work, and it helps you to exercise your time management skills. In college, students will have fewer class times and more free time. Having a free block familiarizes you with college life earlier, and you will become better at using your free time wisely. In addition, here are some of my personal perspectives that might be helpful: 1. Perfectionism is often detrimental. Don’t set too many goals and try to achieve every one of them. Know your priorities, which might be your grades or sport, and put most of the effort into that. 2. Having a good mood boosts your productivity. Getting some sunlight, staying hydrated, and eating enough usually makes the mood better. Most importantly, don’t be afraid to talk to your friends, parents, and the counselors at the health center when you are having an especially bad week. 3. Be honest about how much sleep you need. Only a few people can sustain themselves with very little sleep. Sacrificing sleep often compromises efficiency, ending up worsening the results compared to getting enough sleep. Try not to drink coffee after 3 PM. Caffeine could stay in your body and hurt your sleep quality. Getting through junior year not only requires better time management but also better mood, lifestyle, and mindset management. Believe me: the start is always the hardest. The further you progress into the year, the better you get. Good luck to all of you!

When AI provides the claim, the reasoning, and the voice simultaneously, critical thinking is lost. The ethical standard for AI use is human authorship. When juniors write their history thesis, they make several intellectual decisions: choosing the question, framing the claim, and selecting the evidence. They take full responsibility for mistakes because the thinking is theirs. AI undermines authorship when people ask for “the answer” and submit the gathered information instantly and directly, which hands over the process and authority for crafting their response. Education is supposed to build capacity, not just produce output; it’s more than content transfer. Students build judgment through crafting mental models and applying them. They apply their models in school, learn from and refine them based on teacher feedback, and use them to thrive in real-world settings. When one reaches for AI before building that internal model, they skip this developmental work. AI creates a polished page, but you don’t practice the process of producing it. Schools face a structural problem: students adopt AI quickly, but many classrooms still grade products over process. This mismatch rewards exactly the crutch behavior teachers want to discourage. The better response to this “crutch-boom” is structural change, not surveillance. Teachers could grade outlines, drafts, and revisions rather than just final pages. Classes can add in-class checkpoints or graded discussions with impromptu prompts that reward real thinking. These changes will make authorship easier to practice and harder to fake. An AI-rich world will not reward whoever writes fastest; instead, it will reward the ability to judge. It will reward those with the ability to say, here is what I think, here is why, and here is what would change my mind. You can be successful with the facilitation tool of AI, but only if you refuse its most tempting offer: the crutch.

To see what this looks like for the Class of 2026, an anonymous survey was sent out asking seniors to share their post-grad plans. The responses included a little bit of everything, from internships and jobs to travel, rest, and fun. Some students are planning on taking on internships or career-focused programs. For some, this summer is all about preparing for the future. Internships and training programs are a popular choice for students looking to gain experience before college begins. One senior shared that they are doing an “EMT training course during the week and working at a restaurant on weekends,” while another said, “I’m planning to go to the gym, complete an internship, and get myself prepared for college.” These plans show that even during summer break, many students are still focused on growth and preparation, using their time to build skills, explore interests, and take meaningful steps toward their future careers. Many seniors are spending part of their summer working, whether it’s for extra cash or just something to do. From restaurants and retail to lifeguarding, seniors are stepping into all kinds of different jobs. One student described working at a marina for the third summer, helping with boats and assisting customers. One senior is coming back to Govs over the summer, working with Govs Plus, where she will be teaching classes and mentoring students. One student is planning on caddying, while another plans to work at a boutique in Nantucket. Whether it’s saving money for college or just gaining independence, these jobs are a big part of many students’ summers. Travel and relaxation are just as important, with students planning trips to other continents, going to concerts, heading to the beach, and spending time with loved ones. People are traveling to a wide variety of places, including Cape Cod, Nantucket, Japan, Florida, Greece, and Italy. One student wrote that they were just planning on sleeping, saying, “Let a man rest.” After four years of hard work at Govs, no one can argue with that. One student even wrote that “I’m going to become homeless exploring the world… then come back at the end of the summer and become a billionaire.” A plan that ambitious definitely captures the spirit of senior summer! In the end, this summer is all about transition. Whether seniors are working, traveling, interning, or just relaxing, the choices they make reflect not only what they want to do, but who they are becoming. Each plan offers insight into their priorities, ambitions, and personalities at this turning point in their lives. Before everyone heads off in different directions for college, this summer will be a time to make memories, try new things, and enjoy a well-deserved break.

Teenagers naturally fall asleep later at night and need between eight and ten hours of rest to function properly. This lines up with what science tells us. The CDC states that adolescent brains need 8-10 hours of sleep to undergo a shift in their internal clocks during puberty, pushing their natural sleep and wake cycles later. Asking a teenager to perform complex thinking at 8:15 a.m. is very challenging. When school starts early in the morning, most students simply are not getting enough time for homework, athletics, dinner, and socializing. A recent survey conducted among students at Gov’s revealed that a majority feel very tired during first blocks (M/Tu/W/F) and feel much better during their Thursday A block, which starts an hour later. Students feel they will be able to be more alert, motivated, and focused later in the day rather than the early morning hours. Many say they regularly arrive at school having slept fewer than seven hours. Mrs. Kingsbury expressed the difficulties with how the schedule is laid out and how it affects Govs students’ academics and afterschool programs. She pointed out that the current schedule does not align with what research shows about teenage sleep needs or the times of day when adolescent brains are most capable of learning. Students are being asked to engage when it neurologically is very difficult to understand and comprehend coursework. With all the benefits of starting class later, there are factors that halt the deans and others from making this change. Many parents rely on an early start time to fit their own work schedule and a later dismissal could interfere with afterschool activities that require referee availability, maintenance staff, and athletic trainers. With many outside factors affecting this decision, it makes large scale change very hard to implement. So what could a solution look like? From the survey, many students believe pushing the start time back even fifteen to forty-five minutes could make a meaningful difference. A later start around 8:45-9:15 would allow students to arrive more rested, more focused, and genuinely ready to learn. For Govs, we could shorten PA to only be an hour with a 25 minute lunch or shorten passing time to 5 minutes. Moving everything up in the day by a couple hours would allow for afternoon programs to finish up on time and the evening routine of dinner and study hall to take place. Academic performance, mental health, and student wellbeing are all directly tied to how much sleep students get. If Govs wants its students performing at their best, it may be time to rethink when the day begins.

Patty had a rare mix of efficiency and intentional care. Walking away from the counter left you with more than just a meal; you left with joy knowing that the food you have been given has been made with love.

articles.title: A New Dress Code for an Old School

Some in the community were critical because they thought it presented a false sense of what the Govs experience would be to the prospective students. But perhaps this is how we should look every day so that we can honor the history and beauty of the campus. Looking presentable on a day like Accepted Students Day is crucial because it sends a strong, positive message to the new kids and parents. The way we present ourselves contributes to how others perceive not just individual students, but the entire community. But it can also affect how we see ourselves and our place in the long tradition of GDA. We sent out a survey asking if Govs should have a stricter dress code or not, and 160 people responded. Overall, 60% said we should keep the current dress code, and 40% wanted something more formal. Of the faculty that responded, 75% of the responses were in favor of a stricter dress code. This survey does not conclusively suggest that we should reinstate a stronger dress code, but it does hint at a desire to consider some changes to the rules we have now. The school has replaced tradition with comfort, and we are not better for it. Part of the appeal of prep schools is that they are preppy. When you dress well, you feel good, and that translates to increased confidence inside and outside of the classroom. We should strive to be a school that is better dressed than the eighth graders coming for tours. Coeducation through 2015 –For girls: dresses or collared shirts with skirts or pants. –Shirts could not show shoulders. –For boys: slacks (no jeans) with collared shirt and belt. –No hats allowed inside buildings. –Struggle with enforcement. Current Day –Gender Neutral dress code. –”Must look presentable,” but few other guidelines.

articles.title: Navigating the Course Selection Process
paras: Every spring, students enter one of the most challenging and chaotic times of the year…course selection. What seems like a simple “pick your classes” situation quickly turns into a stressful experience that feels like doing a thousand-piece puzzle. The biggest issue, though, is that no one knows what is going on. These are some of the biggest challenges for students who are navigating the course selection process:

1. Course Selection Convocation: There are many problems with this. It happens at 8:15 on a Thursday morning, when no one is awake and able to think about their future. Then all the department heads go up and project a slide that organizes the classes that no one understands. By the time it’s over, students leave feeling overwhelmed, overtired, and even more confused than they were before.

The appeal process: Students scroll through online documents with vague descriptions and extraneous prerequisites. They stumble upon big words like ‘Department Placements’ and ‘appeal,’ which might as well mean ‘good luck.’ At some point, it starts feeling less like course selection and more like a test you didn’t study for. 3. Your advisor has no idea what is actually going on: You meet with them and leave feeling confident in your classes, only to question every decision you have made since 6th grade the next minute. Sure…your advisor might, if you’re lucky, bring you donuts, but can they tell you about computer science or robotics and give you a suggestion that will actually work? The short answer is…no? 4. The scheduling conflict: You think you have just found the perfect class. It’s something you’re interested in, the teacher is not too hard, and it looks good for college. Then you realize it is actually a semester-long class that doesn’t fit your schedule. Cool. 5. No APs: To top it all off, there is the big question: What will APs look like next year? Administrators dance around the word ‘AP,’ phasing in ‘Advanced’ instead, and no one knows what that might mean or when that might happen. For years, AP exams have been long seen as the highest academic honor—challenging and slightly terrifying. With the school now trying to move away from AP classes, students are left with questions about what will replace them and if those classes will carry the same weight. In the end, the course selection process is about making the best decisions for your future self with the (little) information that you have. Maybe the lesson here is not to build the perfect schedule, but to learn to navigate difficult decisions and accept that sometimes you might have to just throw in the towel and “trust” the process because somehow, it always ends up okay.

Why move my life somewhere else if I can just commute every day? After four years of sticking it out and serving as a dorm proctor, I can honestly say that I made the right decision. My experience has been mostly positive, though there are positives to both the boarding and day student experiences. One difference between boarders and day students is the access to resources on campus. When you are boarding, your life revolves around campus. It is easy to access the library throughout the day and no hassle to meet with teachers after afternoon program. You can even go to the dining hall for a quick snack. There is a good deal of convenience when it comes to being on campus. On the other hand, Reese ‘26 proposed that though day students might not be as involved at Govs, they get to enjoy a more flexible schedule. “Day students get to go anywhere after their commitments,” she said. Which made me think… day students can escape the chaos that can be right in the center of Govs, including tests, busy schedules, or friend drama. They can spend their time outside of the Byfield bubble, whereas for boarders, it’s more difficult to get off campus. Another difference between borders and day students is the difference in community. Govs becomes the boarders’ community. They spend most of their time at school during the school year. Whether you are 30 minutes or 15 hours away from home, the connections you make in the dorm and on campus truly mean a lot, with late- night talks, ramen night, and a constant support system. Juliana Lucero ‘26 said, “Coming in as a freshman, the dorm community was one of the greatest support systems I had here.” However, Reese ‘26 brought up the fact that though you can make a new community at school, you don’t get to interact with your community at home. Some of us have staples in our lives–mainly family–that help us get through day by day. When you are away from those constants, school can be hard. Reese highlighted that going home to her family helps her create stability in her routine. Besides the challenges and disadvantages, I wouldn’t change one thing. The dorm community has become a second home for me, and I’ll forever cherish these four years. Though I haven’t had the flexibility to go off campus consistently or see my family as often as I wanted, boarding here at Govs has helped me grow as a person and a leader.

articles.title: The True Crime Elective
paras: When I was 10, I got my first crime novel for Christmas: Sherlock Holmes. It was a classic: intriguing, sophisticated, and full of twists that a 10-year-old would never expect. The murderers were more than just “bad people”; they had their own tragedies, and their crimes became acts of desperation.

This spring, Ms. Davis started a new elective called “True Crime as Novels.” I got to know this class through Cecileah Wang ‘26, who told me the class is different from her past English classes because “This class isn’t really about analyzing the writing style or the historical period, but more like how the killer thinks in that moment.” I interviewed Ms. Davis and asked her some questions about the class.

JL: What inspired you to teach this class? Ms. Davis: I loved true crime myself. I’ve watched all the HBO and Netflix true crime shows. I’ve also talked to multiple kids, and they seemed interested in this topic. I thought this class would be a great way to connect true crime with literature. JL: What is a book you are teaching? Ms. Davis: The first book I’m teaching is The Fact of a Body: A Murder and a Memoir, which tells the story of Ricky Langley, who murdered a six-year-old boy in Louisiana in 1992. It follows the author’s perspective as a law student who wants to fight the death penalty. But as she goes deeper into Langley’s case, she realizes she wants him to die, while also exploring her own childhood memory of being abused by her grandfather. JL: What is something you find interesting about antagonists in these books? Ms. Davis: One thing I find interesting about these true crime novels is that the antagonists are more relatable than I expected. These serial killers are not simply black and white, good or evil, guilty or innocent. The reason this book is so uncomfortable is that we get the whole story about the murderer. He has a difficult upbringing and serious mental health issues. There are times when he is humanized, and it feels really uncomfortable. JL: How does point of view in these books impact us as readers? Ms. Davis: Another thing I think is very interesting about good literature is that the author can manipulate you. The book is written from many perspectives. You move from the crime scene, disgusted by the brutality, to the mom who lost her son, feeling angry and sad. You are drawn to wherever the author wants to take you. The POV of each book or documentary depends on the author or director, and how the story is presented really depends on what they want you to know. JL: Are you teaching this class again in the future? Ms. Davis: Definitely. The English department requires us to rotate classes every year, but I will definitely come back to this class in the future.

Overall, the new changes provide easier maneuverability through the servery area to help people get their food quicker.

While not necessarily serving as a direct cause of Parkinson’s Disease (PD), studies have shown that patients with PD often have elevated levels of TET2, demonstrating an interesting correlation. We followed the research trail through scientific journals for months, uncovering TET2’s normal mechanisms and disease pathway, as well as a hopeful potential treatment for PD – SIRT1 (Silence information regulator 1). In simple terms, SIRT1 might help treat PD by lowering both the amount and activity of TET2. For quite a while, the team seriously (and we mean seriously) considered making removable tattoo stickers for distribution at the conference, for the pronunciation of “TET2” sounds very much like “tattoo.” In fact, this coincidence was one of the reasons the protein triumphed during its original competition with other proteins when the team was trying to decide which to research. Other reasons include the fact that PD is a major public health problem that affects as many as one million Americans in any given year, and that TET2 is a critical regulator of DNA methylation, which basically means that it can serve as a light switch that turns the light – in this case, DNA – on and off. Pretty important stuff. At the conference, we explained all of this and more (minus the tattoo stickers). We had a stunning 3D-printed protein model and a massive science poster created by the team to help illustrate our presentation in great detail. One of our listeners – an elderly scientist – told the team: “My husband is diagnosed with Parkinson’s, so it is just great to see you young people doing this work.” We were genuinely touched. Her comment was why we were so happy and willing to devote all the long hours of work – not only to grow and learn, but also to contribute to a change that could make a real impact. Of course, we were also very happy and willing to do our work because every Wednesday, we played board games with Dr. Alex. Every day, the team is immersed in chattering and laughter even at the most random jokes. You’ll find more about these if you join the team for the winter season next year. So why not give it a shot?
